walkthroughs.body_html:
Big businesses split work into departments:

  • Marketing — promotes products.
  • Finance — counts the money.
  • HR — looks after staff.
  • Operations — makes the product.

Front-line staff meet customers — shop floor, tills, call centre.

Back-office staff support them — payroll, IT, buying stock.

Both matter — no one works alone.

A business hierarchy is its layers:

  • Directors set the big plan.
  • Managers run teams.
  • Team members do the daily work.

Like a triangle: few at the top, many at the bottom. 🔺

mcqs.q: Is the manager the person who does the most work in a team?
options: Front-line staff are soldiers employed by shops.
Not necessarily — managers plan, organise, support and check the team's work; their job is making others effective rather than doing every task themselves.
Managers are just the busiest workers.
Managers are chosen because they are the tallest.

mcqs.q: Do directors and managers do the same job?
options: Front-line staff are soldiers employed by shops.
Director is just a fancier word for manager.
Directors only direct films.
No — directors set the long-term direction and major decisions of the business, while managers organise the day-to-day work needed to deliver those plans.

mcqs.q: Are front-line staff less important than office staff?
options: Managers are chosen because they are the tallest.
Jobs you can't see, like back-office work, matter more than serving customers.
Front-line staff are soldiers employed by shops.
No — front-line staff deal directly with customers and shape the firm's reputation, while back-office roles support them; both are needed for the business to work.
